question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Sharp, substernal chest pain worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward" -> "Pericarditis symptoms" -> "High-pitched rubbing sound on cardiac exam" -> "Pericardial friction rub" -> "Depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations on ECG" -> "Pericarditis" -> "Dressler syndrome" -> 95%

enhanced_information: The patient's symptoms of sharp, substernal chest pain worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward, along with pericardial friction rub and ECG findings of depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations, are consistent with pericarditis. Dressler syndrome is the most likely cause given the history of recent illness and the presence of these specific symptoms and findings.
analysis: The patient's presentation of sharp, substernal chest pain worsened by inspiration and relieved by leaning forward, along with pericardial friction rub and ECG findings of depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations, is classic for pericarditis. Dressler syndrome, which is post-myocardial infarction pericarditis, is the most likely cause in this scenario given the recent illness history and specific symptoms and findings.
